title: Nocturnes (Nuages, Fêtes, Sirènes)
hook: Three night pictures in sound, named after Whistler’s paintings, with drifting clouds, a festival with a passing parade, and the sirens singing over the sea.

painting.title: Nocturne in Blue and Silver
painting.collection: Harvard Art Museums (Fogg Museum), Cambridge, Massachusetts
painting.pairingNote: Debussy named his Nocturnes after Whistler’s night paintings like this one, a river dissolving into blue and silver mist, and called his own music a study in grey, as a painter would.

facts: The title does not mean the gentle piano nocturnes of Chopin. Debussy took it from the American painter James McNeill Whistler, who called his misty night views of the Thames “nocturnes”. Debussy said the word should be heard in a “decorative” sense: the impressions and special effects of light that it suggests.

The work took him seven years. It began around 1892 as “Three Scenes at Twilight”; in 1894 he planned it as a piece for the violinist Eugène Ysaÿe with orchestra, describing it as an experiment with a single colour, “what a study in grey would be in painting”. In the end he wrote it for full orchestra and finished the score on 15 December 1899. He told his publisher that it was harder than writing a five-act opera.

*Nuages* and *Fêtes* were first played in Paris on 9 December 1900 by the Lamoureux Orchestra under Camille Chevillard. *Sirènes* had to wait until 27 October 1901, because the women’s choir it needs was not available. Debussy went on revising the score almost until he died.

Each piece has a small story from Debussy himself. *Nuages* came to him on a stormy day, crossing the Pont de la Concorde in Paris: clouds driven by the wind and a boat’s horn. *Fêtes* remembers a festival in the Bois de Boulogne, with a military band marching through the crowd. *Sirènes* is the sea, and the song of the sirens, sung by women’s voices without words.
bigPicture.inOneLine: grey clouds moving slowly across the sky (I), a bright, whirling festival with a parade passing through (II), the sea at night and the sirens’ wordless song (III).

movements.heading: Nuages
movements.title: Nuages (Clouds)
movements.summary: Debussy described “the unchanging aspect of the sky” and the slow, solemn movement of clouds, fading in grey tinged with white. A winding figure in the woodwinds drifts across the orchestra; a cor anglais answers with a short, sad call, like a boat’s horn heard across the river. In the middle, flute and harp sing a simple tune together. Nothing ever gets loud.

mainIdeas.name: The clouds
mainIdeas.description: a slow, rocking figure for clarinets and bassoons, moving in parallel chords.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: a short, falling phrase on the cor anglais, each time a little different.

mainIdeas.name: The middle tune
mainIdeas.description: a plain melody played by flute and harp in unison, built on the five notes of the [[pentatonic-scale|pentatonic scale]].

stops.hear: Clarinets and bassoons play a slow, swaying line in pale, parallel chords
The cor anglais calls with a short, drooping phrase; a horn answers softly
Soft chords in the strings, divided into many parts, slide past one another
The cor anglais returns over a faint, restless murmur
stops.happening: The call heard again from further away

stops.hear: Flute and harp together play a simple, almost folk-like tune
stops.happening: The middle section, on the [[pentatonic-scale|pentatonic scale]]

stops.hear: The strings take up the tune, then the winding cloud figure returns

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Fragments of the horn call and the flute tune; a soft drum roll and low strings fade to nothing

notice: Count how often the cor anglais call returns, and listen to how it changes. It is the only clear “voice” in a landscape of soft chords.

movements.heading: Fêtes
movements.title: Fêtes (Festivals)
movements.summary: Debussy wrote of the “vibrating, dancing rhythm” of the air, with sudden flashes of light. The orchestra whirls in fast triplets. Then, from far away, a procession approaches: a quiet march rhythm on harps, drums and plucked basses, muted trumpets playing a fanfare, louder and louder until it fills the scene. The festival swallows the parade and slowly scatters.

mainIdeas.name: The whirl
mainIdeas.description: fast, repeated three-note figures in the strings, with dancing tunes in the woodwinds on top.

mainIdeas.name: The procession
mainIdeas.description: a march heard first in the distance, played by three muted trumpets over a soft, steady beat.

stops.hear: The violins hammer out a fast, three-note figure; sudden chords flash across it
A lively, dancing tune in the cor anglais and clarinets
The music swirls and grows, with sudden bright outbursts
Almost silence: a soft, steady march beat in the harps, timpani and plucked basses
Three [[muted|muted]] trumpets play a fanfare in the distance
The march grows to full volume with trombones, and the festival music joins it
stops.happening: The parade passes right through the crowd

stops.hear: The whirling festival music returns

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music thins out and grows quiet, in short, fading bursts
stops.happening: The crowd scatters into the night

notice: Listen for the march from the moment the harps and drums start their quiet beat. Debussy builds a whole procession in sound, from far away to right in front of you.

movements.heading: Sirènes
movements.title: Sirènes (Sirens)
movements.summary: The sea, with its countless rhythms, and the sirens’ song among the moonlit waves. A small choir of women joins the orchestra, singing without words, on the open sound of a vowel. Their two-note swaying phrase rises and falls like the waves. In the middle the sea grows rougher; at the end the voices drift away, “laughing” as they pass, in Debussy’s words.

mainIdeas.name: The waves
mainIdeas.description: rocking figures in the strings and harps, never quite still.

mainIdeas.name: The sirens
mainIdeas.description: women’s voices in a [[vocalise|vocalise]], a melody sung without words, often just two notes swinging back and forth.

stops.hear: Rippling harps and strings, with soft calls in the woodwinds and horns
Women’s voices, softly, on a swaying two-note phrase
stops.happening: The sirens begin their song, a [[vocalise|vocalise]]

stops.hear: The voices spread into a longer, wider melody; the waves grow
stops.happening: The song draws the listener in

stops.hear: The music quickens and swells; brass and voices together
The fullest moment, voices and orchestra at their brightest
Calmer again: the rocking returns, the voices softer
Everything slows down and thins out
stops.happening: *Plus lent*, holding back to the end

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The voices fade one by one into the sound of the sea

notice: The voices are used like instruments. Try to hear where the choir stops and the orchestra begins; often you cannot tell.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Abbado recorded the *Nocturnes* in Symphony Hall, Boston, in February 1970, with the women of the New England Conservatory Chorus prepared by Lorna Cooke deVaron. On the Spotify album the *Nocturnes* are tracks 1–3, followed by Ravel and Scriabin.

threads.title: Painting with sound
threads.body: The titles describe light and movement rather than events. Debussy borrowed his title from a painter who had borrowed it from music.

threads.title: Never finished
threads.body: Debussy worked on the *Nocturnes* for seven years before they were published, and kept correcting and re-colouring the orchestration for years afterwards. A definitive edition appeared only in 1930, twelve years after his death.

threads.title: Darkness to light to night
threads.body: Grey sky, a blaze of festival lights, and the moonlit sea: three moods of the same night.
